newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Birla Yamaha says 96/97 net to surge.
newsitem.headline: India's Birla Yamaha says 96/97 net to surge.

text.p: Diesel generator maker Birla Yamaha Ltd expects to make a net profit of some 100 million rupees ($2.8 million) in 1996/97 by cashing in on an acute power shortage in India, a senior company official said on Wednesday.
"This year's results will be announced shortly. We'll be touching a net profit close to 100 million rupees," S. Rajagopalan, vice-president of marketing and sales, told Reuters.
He said the firm's profit totalled 60.4 million rupees the year earlier which ended on March 31, 1996.

The firm, a joint venture between India's Birla family and Japan's Yamaha Motor Co, predicted a sharp surge in its net just a year after it wiped out accumulated losses that ran to more than 21 million rupees.
The Birlas hold a 40 percent stake and Yamaha 26 percent. The rest is held by financial institutions and the public.
"The main reason for our losses was the interest burden on foreign capital loans taken in 1986, which kept increasing with yen-rupee appreciation," Rajagopalan said.
With financial support from Yamaha and a repayment waiver from financial institutions, the company turned the corner in 1995/96 and never looked back, he said.
"Turnover this year, we will be able to touch around 900 million rupees," Rajagopalan said. Sales in 1995/96 totalled 692.5 million rupees, he said.
"We have further consolidated ourselves. It is a very happy situation," Rajagopalan said.

The company's improving performance has been driven by a severe power shortage in India, where daily power cuts last for several hours. Birla Yamaha controlled about 40 percent of the power generator market, Rajagopalan said.
"At least for the next four years, the power scenario continues to be favourable for the generator set industry," he said. Birla Yamaha expects the sector to expand by up to 15 percent annually.

Export orders from Yamaha were crucial for the Indian venture's new-found profitability, Rajagopalan said. The company exported about 35 percent of its production in both 1995/96 and 1996/97, all under the Yamaha brand name, he said.
